chunks: "I'll describe an N-channel enhancement MOSFET. You start with a P-type silicon body and two heavily doped N-type regions, the source and drain.
Between them, on top of the silicon, there's a thin insulating oxide with a conductive gate on top.
With the gate at zero, going from source to drain you hit N, then P, then N, so it's two back-to-back diodes and no current flows. Now put a positive voltage on the gate.
The gate and the silicon form a capacitor. First, the positive gate pushes the holes in the P-type body away from the surface, leaving a depletion region.
Push harder, past the threshold voltage, and the field pulls enough electrons to the surface that it effectively flips to N-type right under the gate.
That thin inversion layer is the channel, and now there's a continuous N-type path from source to drain. Then V DS pushes electrons from source to drain through that channel.
The more gate voltage above threshold, the more channel charge, so the lower the resistance. That's the triode region.
If you keep increasing V DS , the voltage between gate and channel at the drain end drops until the channel pinches off there.
After that, extra drain voltage doesn't add current, so it saturates at about 1 over 2 k n(V GS-V t) squared .
The key thing is that the gate never conducts: it controls the channel purely through the electric field, which is where the name 'field-effect transistor' comes from."
